question: Who does the manual say should attempt to carry passengers or large loads?
choice_b: Passenger weight has no effect on handling
choice_c: Only riders who have never taken a passenger before
choice_d: Only experienced riders, since extra weight affects handling and requires extra practice, preparation, and caution
explanation: The extra weight of a passenger or cargo affects how the motorcycle handles, requiring extra practice, preparation and caution; for this reason, only experienced riders should attempt to carry passengers or large loads.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.36, 'Carrying Passengers and Cargo'

question: Before carrying a passenger, what should a rider check regarding tire pressure?
choice_a: Check the air pressure of both tires, not just the rear, per the owner's manual or the motorcycle's label
choice_b: Only the rear tire needs checking since it carries the extra weight
choice_c: Tire pressure never needs adjustment for a passenger
choice_d: Deflate both tires slightly for a softer ride
explanation: Check the air pressure of both tires; though most added weight will typically be on the rear wheel, don't forget to also check the pressure on the front tire, referring to the owner's manual or the label affixed to the motorcycle.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.36-37, 'Preparing Your Motorcycle'

question: How should a rider check and adjust the headlight before carrying a passenger and full load?
choice_a: Headlight aim never needs adjustment for load
choice_b: Mark the unloaded headlight beam position on a wall, then recheck with a full load and passenger, adjusting the beam to match
choice_c: Only check the headlight after dark
choice_d: Remove the headlight when carrying passengers
explanation: Prior to loading, position the motorcycle about 10 feet from a wall in an unlighted garage and mark the headlight beam location; with a full load and passenger, recheck the beam location and use the adjusting screws to lower the beam to the same height.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.37, 'Preparing Your Motorcycle'

question: What equipment should be in place before carrying a passenger, according to the manual?
choice_a: No special equipment is needed for passengers
choice_b: Only a helmet for the passenger, nothing else
choice_c: Passenger footrests, a proper seat large enough for both riders, and a strap or solid handholds for the passenger
choice_d: A sidecar is required for any passenger
explanation: Be sure the motorcycle is equipped with passenger footrests, has a proper seat large enough to hold both rider and passenger without crowding, and has a strap or solid handholds for the passenger to hold onto.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.37, 'Equipment for Carrying a Passenger'

question: Where should a child be seated on a motorcycle, and why?
choice_a: In front of the rider for better visibility
choice_b: On the fuel tank for the best view
choice_c: Seating position for children makes no difference
choice_d: Immediately behind the rider, since a child sitting in front cannot properly balance and may interfere with the rider's control
explanation: Children should be placed immediately behind the rider; a child sitting in front of the rider will not be able to properly balance and may interfere with the rider's control of the motorcycle.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.37, 'Preparing Your Passenger to Ride'

question: What should a rider tell a passenger to do while mounting the motorcycle?
choice_a: Get on only after the engine has started and the transmission is in neutral, while the rider keeps both feet on the ground and the front brake applied
choice_b: Mount before the engine is started
choice_c: Mount from the left side only, regardless of traffic
choice_d: It doesn't matter when a passenger mounts
explanation: Tell your passenger to get on the motorcycle only after you have started the engine and have the transmission in neutral; as the passenger mounts, keep both your feet on the ground and the front brake applied.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.37, 'Preparing Your Passenger to Ride'

question: What should a passenger be instructed to do through turns and curves?
choice_a: Lean opposite the rider to counterbalance
choice_b: Stay directly behind the rider and lean with the rider through turns and curves
explanation: The passenger should stay directly behind the rider and lean with the rider through turns and curves; it is helpful for the passenger to look over the rider's shoulder in the direction of the turn.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.37, 'Preparing Your Passenger to Ride'

question: Why should a passenger keep both feet firmly on the footrests, even when stopped?
choice_a: It is only a comfort preference with no safety purpose
choice_b: Footrests are only needed while moving, not when stopped
choice_c: Firm footing prevents the passenger from falling off and pulling the rider off
choice_d: It helps the passenger see over the rider's shoulder
explanation: Keep both feet firmly on the footrests, even when stopped -- firm footing will prevent your passenger from falling off and pulling you off.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.37, 'Preparing Your Passenger to Ride'

question: How does riding with a passenger affect a motorcycle's handling?
choice_a: A passenger has no measurable effect on handling
choice_b: A passenger always makes the motorcycle faster to stop
choice_c: A passenger only affects fuel economy, not handling
choice_d: The heavier the passenger, the longer it may take to speed up, slow down, or turn
explanation: A motorcycle will respond differently when riding with a passenger; the heavier the passenger, the longer it may take to speed up, slow down, or turn.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.38, 'Riding With Passengers'

question: What does the manual recommend when riding with a passenger regarding gaps in traffic?
choice_a: Wait for larger gaps to cross, enter, or merge in traffic
choice_b: Use the same size gaps as when riding solo
choice_c: Take smaller gaps since two riders are more visible
choice_d: Gap size is irrelevant with a passenger aboard
explanation: When riding with passengers, wait for larger gaps to cross, enter, or merge in traffic, and start slowing earlier as you approach a stop.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.38, 'Riding With Passengers'

question: Where should loads ideally be placed on a motorcycle, according to the manual?
choice_a: As far behind the rear axle as possible for balance
choice_b: Over or in front of the rear axle, since mounting loads behind the rear axle can affect turning and braking and cause a wobble
choice_c: On the handlebars for easy access
choice_d: Load placement has no effect on handling
explanation: Try to place the load over, or in front of, the rear axle -- mounting loads behind the rear axle can affect how the motorcycle turns and brakes, and can also cause a wobble.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.38-39, 'Carrying Loads'

question: Why does the manual recommend securing loads low or in saddlebags rather than high?
choice_a: High-mounted loads are always more aerodynamic
choice_b: Load height has no effect on balance
choice_c: Attaching a load higher raises the motorcycle's center of gravity and can upset its balance
explanation: Secure loads low, or put them in saddlebags -- attaching a load higher raises the motorcycle's center of gravity and can upset its balance.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.39, 'Carrying Loads'

question: What can an uneven load in saddlebags cause?
choice_a: An uneven load has no effect on handling
choice_c: It only affects the motorcycle's top speed
choice_d: It can cause the motorcycle to pull to one side, and overloading may cause the bags to catch in the wheel or chain, locking the rear wheel
explanation: If you use saddlebags, load each with about the same weight -- an uneven load can cause the motorcycle to pull to one side, and overloading may cause the bags to catch in the wheel or chain, locking the rear wheel and causing a skid.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.39, 'Carrying Loads'

question: Before a long trip with a fully loaded motorcycle, what does the manual recommend doing first?
choice_a: Take a test ride through familiar neighborhood roads to check the suspension settings and make sure nothing scrapes or restricts steering
choice_b: Go straight to the highway to test the load at high speed
choice_c: Skip any test ride to save time
choice_d: Remove the load and ride without it first, then add it back only at the destination
explanation: Prior to starting out, take a test ride with your fully loaded motorcycle through familiar neighborhood roads to get a feel for the operation, making sure the suspension settings are correct and that the side stand, footrests, and exhaust pipes don't scrape in turns.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.39, 'Pre-Ride Test'
